summary: Year 5 learners reflect and translate a scalene shape on a squared/coordinate grid, state the image coordinates as (across, up), and justify that the moved shape is congruent — same size and shape, with only its position (and, for reflection, its sense) changed. The core idea is that a transformation is a precise rule for where every point goes: reflection sends each vertex perpendicularly across the mirror line to an equal distance on the far side, and translation sends every vertex the same distance in the same direction. Congruence is the invariant that makes both trustworthy.
misconceptions: Reflecting by sliding the shape across the mirror unchanged, so its sense is not reversed (translate-instead-of-flip).
Placing the image the wrong distance from the mirror — not equidistant — often by miscounting or letting the shape touch the line.
Believing the shape changes size or becomes a 'different shape' once moved, rather than staying congruent.
Reversing the image coordinates (writing y before x) when reporting where the shape landed.

activities.title: Build a reflection vertex by vertex using the perpendicular-equidistant rule
steps: Start with a scalene triangle on a squared grid and a vertical mirror line two squares to its right (choose scalene so a reversal of sense is visible).

For each vertex in turn, draw the line from the vertex to the mirror line that meets the mirror at a right angle (perpendicular to the mirror line); with this vertical mirror it runs along a horizontal grid line. Check the right angle rather than assuming it.
Count the squares from the vertex to the mirror along that perpendicular, then count the SAME number of squares beyond the mirror and mark the image vertex there.
Repeat for every vertex, then join the image vertices to complete the reflected shape.

Compare the vertex order: check that the image reads the mirror-image way round (a clockwise order of corners becomes anticlockwise) — this reversed 'sense' is what makes it a true reflection rather than a slide.
State the coordinates of each image corner as (across, up), reading across first then up.
activities.insight: A reflection is produced point by point: every line joining an object vertex to its image is perpendicular to the mirror line, and the image vertex is the same distance beyond the mirror as the object is in front. Because this reverses the vertex order, the shape's sense flips — distinguishing a genuine reflection from a shape merely slid across.

activities.title: Translate every point by the same vector and contrast it with reflection
steps: Take the original triangle and set a single translation rule, e.g. '5 squares right, 2 squares up', shown as a staircase arrow.
Apply that identical move to ONE vertex first, then check that every other vertex has to follow the exact same move.
Complete the translated shape and confirm its orientation and sense are unchanged (it reads the same way round as the original).
Place the reflected shape and the translated shape side by side and describe the felt difference: the slide keeps sense, the flip reverses it.
Report the translated image coordinates as (across, up).
activities.insight: A translation moves every point the same distance in the same direction, so orientation and sense are unchanged — the opposite of reflection, which reverses sense. Both leave the shape congruent to the original.

activities.title: Test congruence by tracing and overlaying
steps: Trace the original triangle onto tracing paper (or cut out a card copy, noting that real paper/card has slight thickness and only approximates the ideal zero-thickness flat figure it represents).

Lay the tracing directly over the translated image and confirm an exact match in size and shape; for the reflected image, turn the tracing paper OVER to make it match — this flip is itself the reversed sense, and the size and shape are still identical.
Say aloud that the moved shape is congruent to the original: only its position (and, for the reflection, its sense) has changed, not its size or shape.
Answer the challenge 'Is it a new, different triangle now?' — about the mathematical shape represented — by pointing to the exact overlay match.
activities.insight: Reflection and translation change where a shape is (and reflection changes which way round it reads) but never its size or shape; the technical word for this sameness is 'congruent'.

activities.title: Diagnostic performance task: reflect, translate, and justify
steps: Given a squared grid showing a scalene triangle and a vertical mirror line two squares to its right, reflect the triangle in the mirror line and state the coordinates of the reflected corners as (across, up).
Back with the original, translate it 5 squares right and 2 squares up, and describe the move made.
Explain whether the new triangle is the same as the first and how you know, using tracing/overlay and the word congruent.

Answer probes: What is the relationship between the line joining a corner to its image and the mirror line? If the mirror moved one square further right, what would happen to the reflected triangle? If a friend slid the triangle across without turning it, is that a reflection, and how can you tell?
activities.insight: Holding the perpendicular-equidistant rule produces an image that is both the correct distance AND reversed in sense; merely sliding produces the wrong sense (and often the wrong distance). Watching HOW the image is assembled — perpendicular vertex by vertex, or shunted as a whole block — separates understanding from imitation, and the congruence question separates learners who see the shape as invariant from those who think moving changes it.

checkQuestion: Hand the child a squared grid showing a scalene triangle and a vertical mirror line two squares to its right. Say: 'Reflect this triangle in the mirror line, then tell me the coordinates of the reflected corners. Now, back with the original, translate it 5 squares right and 2 squares up and describe the move you made. Last, tell me: is your new triangle the same as the first one, and how do you know?' Set the task and WATCH how the image is built — do not explain the rule.
checkAnswer: The child places each reflected vertex perpendicularly opposite its original at an equal number of squares beyond the mirror line, so the image is equidistant and its sense is reversed (a scalene triangle visibly reads the other way round); reports the image coordinates as (across, up); translates by moving every vertex 5 right and 2 up together; and states the moved shape is congruent — same size and shape — checking by matching or tracing, understanding only position (and, for the reflection, orientation/sense) changed.
